guest.bio_context: Carley Weissert is a confidence coach who helps people find their voice and step into their power. She underwent a significant personal transformation starting in fall 2019, intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic, involving deep personal development work, healing from patterns of people-pleasing and perfectionism, and ultimately ending her marriage about two years prior to this interview. She describes herself as having evolved from living according to others' expectations to discovering her authentic self.

context.real_quote: The most impactful thing that you can do as a human is just live in alignment.

pending_qa.q: How does identity attachment prevent personal growth and evolution?
pending_qa.r: Carley explained that she had created a persona that checked all the external boxes—a wife, mother, homeowner with a dog—but realized she had built this life to meet others' expectations rather than her own desires. She noted that things like people-pleasing and always saying yes had worked well for years but eventually stopped working, leaving her questioning 'I don't even know who I am anymore.' She became attached to this constructed identity so completely that she needed to let it go entirely to discover her true self.

pending_qa.q: What role does slowing down and inner work play in navigating major life transitions?
pending_qa.r: Both Carley and the host emphasized that the transition process required a lot of slowing down, getting quiet, being with oneself, and tuning out external opinions and conditioning about how life should look. The host described this as a 'dark night of the soul' experience lasting months to a year, while Carley noted it involved meditation, journaling, and building trust in oneself and one's higher power. Both stressed this was not a quick process but a necessary rite of passage.

pending_qa.q: What is the typical timeline for completing a major life transformation or 'lifequake'?
pending_qa.r: The host referenced author Bruce Fuller's book 'Lifequakes,' which found that most people experience two to three major life interruptions during an average lifespan, and these transformations typically take a four to five-year process to complete. The host noted this was a relief to discover because it normalized the extended timeline, stating 'Mine started a little bit before covid and lasted. I'm still recovering. But yeah, it's like this is normal.'

pending_qa.q: How do people fail to complete major life transitions even after beginning them?
pending_qa.r: The host explained that people who went through lifequakes but didn't fully recover were those who pulled back to their previous position before completing the transition. They returned to the same job, same way of thinking or being, and ended up living a life of apathy rather than making it through to do meaningful things. In contrast, those who saw light at the end of the tunnel and pushed through were able to go on to create fulfilling lives, whether that meant raising great children, building strong families, or pursuing other meaningful pursuits.

pending_qa.q: What is the most impactful contribution a person can make to the world?
pending_qa.r: Carley stated: 'The most impactful thing that you can do as a human is just live in alignment. And like when you're in alignment with your life, whatever that is for you, then you are positively impacting those around you. You're giving permission to other people to make shifts that they need to make for themselves.' She emphasized that living authentically—whether that means raising an incredible human being or pursuing any other aligned passion—is a gift to oneself and others.
